On April 24, 1915, the day before the Allied landings at Gallipoli, Ottoman authorities arrested hundreds of Armenian community leaders and intellectuals in Istanbul. In the months that followed, the government deported the Armenian population of Anatolia toward the Syrian desert, and huge numbers died in massacres, on death marches, and in camps; estimates of the dead range from about 600,000 to more than a million. Assyrian and Greek communities also suffered mass killings and deportations. Most historians, and many governments, including that of the United States since 2021, call the destruction of the Armenians a genocide. The Turkish state rejects that term and describes the deaths as part of a wartime tragedy that struck all the peoples of Anatolia. It is one of the most painful subjects in the region, and the thoughtful traveler of Chapter 2 listens before speaking about it.

On October 30, 1918, the Ottoman government signed an armistice with the Allies aboard a British battleship at Mudros, on the Greek island of Lemnos, just outside the Dardanelles. Two weeks later an Allied fleet sailed up the strait it had failed to force in 1915 and anchored off Istanbul, and Allied troops occupied the city.

docs.title: The Gallipoli Campaign
docs.text:
The Gallipoli Campaign (in Turkish, the battles of Çanakkale) was the Allied attempt in 1915 to force the Dardanelles, capture Istanbul, knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war, and open a sea route to Russia. It began with naval attacks. On March 18, 1915, a great Allied fleet tried to push through the Narrows and lost three battleships to a line of mines laid secretly in the days before; Turks commemorate that day as the Çanakkale Victory. On April 25 the Allies landed troops on the Gallipoli Peninsula: British forces at Cape Helles, its southern tip, while the French made a diversionary landing at Kum Kale on the Asian shore before moving to Helles, and the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, the Anzacs, at the cove that now bears their name. The armies fought for eight months over a few kilometers of ridges and gullies, in summer heat and disease and then winter cold, until the Allies withdrew in December 1915 and January 1916. More than 100,000 men died.

For Turks the campaign is a defining national memory, the defense of the homeland at the gate of the capital. For Australians and New Zealanders it is a founding memory too, commemorated every year on Anzac Day, April 25. And for the history in this chapter, it did one more thing: it made the name of a young Ottoman officer. Chapter 8 tells the campaign in full tomorrow, on the battlefield itself, including the Çanakkale Martyrs' Memorial and the words of reconciliation attributed to Atatürk.

docs.title: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk
docs.text:
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (1881–1938) was the Ottoman army officer who led the Turkish national movement after World War I and became the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey. He was born Mustafa in Salonica (Thessaloniki), the son of a customs clerk; tradition says a mathematics teacher gave him the name Kemal, "perfection." The surname Atatürk, "Father Turk," was given to him by the Turkish parliament in 1934.

On April 25, 1915, he commanded the 19th Division at Gallipoli. When the Anzacs came ashore below the heights, he led his men onto the ridge in time to stop their advance, at enormous cost to his own troops. In August he held the line again. Gallipoli made him a colonel, a hero to his soldiers, and a name the public knew. In May 1919, as the Allies occupied Istanbul and Greek troops landed at Smyrna, he sailed to Samsun on the Black Sea, nominally to restore order, and instead began to organize resistance.

Worked example: one life, one shrinking map. Let's follow Mustafa Kemal's life across the map of Part One, because it traces the empire's end almost exactly. The table lists the places of his life and what became of each.

Years Place What he did there What became of the place 1881 Salonica, an Ottoman city with a Sephardic Jewish majority Born Became Greek in 1912, when he was 31 1890s Monastir Military high school Lost in 1912; today Bitola, in North Macedonia 1899–1905 Istanbul War College and staff college Stayed Turkish; the capital until 1923 1911–1912 Libya Fought the Italian invasion Lost to Italy in 1912 1915 Gallipoli Commanded the 19th Division Held 1919 onward Samsun, then Ankara Organized the national movement Ankara became the capital in 1923 1938 Dolmabahçe Palace, Istanbul Died Buried in Ankara

Every city of his youth ended up outside the country he founded. That may help explain why he built it around a nation and its homeland rather than around an empire.

docs.title: Part Three: From Empire to Republic, 1918–1923
docs.text:
Four Wars, Two Names Each

If the years from 1918 to 1923 blur together, that is normal: several wars, three treaties, and two governments overlap, and each side gives them different names. Hold on to one thread at a time, Smyrna for the Greeks and Ankara for the Turks, and use the treaty sim below to see how it all ended. Most people need two readings to sort this part out.

docs.title: The Greco-Turkish War
docs.text:
The Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922) was the war between Greece and the Turkish nationalist movement over western Anatolia. It began on May 15, 1919, when Greek troops landed at Smyrna (İzmir), with the approval of the Allies meeting at the Paris Peace Conference. Smyrna had a large Greek Orthodox population, and the Greek prime minister, Eleftherios Venizelos, saw a chance to fulfill the Megali Idea. In 1920 the Treaty of Sèvres 🔊 Pronounce SEV-ruh gave Greece Eastern Thrace and the administration of the Smyrna zone. Greek armies pushed deep into Anatolia, until the Turkish nationalists stopped them in a three-week battle on the Sakarya River, in August and September 1921, about 80 km from Ankara. In August 1922 the Turkish army broke the Greek front, and on September 9 it entered Smyrna. Days later a fire destroyed the Greek and Armenian quarters of the city; tens of thousands of Christians fled to the waterfront, and many died. Who set the fire is still disputed, a clear case of Chapter 4's contested history, though many historians attribute it to Turkish forces.

The two sides do not even share a name for the war. In Turkey it is the western front of the War of Independence (Kurtuluş Savaşı, "War of Liberation"), and August 30, the day of the decisive victory in 1922, is a national holiday. In Greece it is the Asia Minor Catastrophe (Mikrasiatiki Katastrofi), the end of three thousand years of Greek life on the Anatolian coast, including the Ionian cities we will see around Ephesus on Day 7. Both armies and irregular bands burned villages and killed civilians as they advanced and retreated. Both names are true to the people who use them.

The war's bitterest result was signed in Lausanne, Switzerland, on January 30, 1923: the Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations. It required the compulsory exchange of the Greek Orthodox Christians living in Turkey for the Muslims living in Greece. About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians, most of whom had already fled in 1922, and about 400,000 Muslims were made to leave homes their families had lived in for centuries, and none could return. Two groups were exempted: the Greek Orthodox of Istanbul who had settled there before October 30, 1918, and the Muslims of Western Thrace, in northeastern Greece. Under the main treaty, the Greek Orthodox of the islands of Imbros and Tenedos, near the mouth of the Dardanelles, were exempted too.

Faith, Not Language

Notice the rule the treaty used to decide who was "Greek" and who was "Turkish": religion, not language. Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians from Cappadocia were sent to Greece, and Greek-speaking Muslims from Crete were sent to Turkey. The millet system of Chapter 6 had sorted people by faith for five centuries, and in its last act it sorted them across a border.

Worked example: the exchange on our route. Let's find the exchange at three of our stops. On Day 9 in Heraklion, the Church of Agios Titos, which had served as a mosque under Ottoman rule, became a church again in 1925, after the city's Muslims had left for Turkey; many of them settled on the Turkish Aegean coast, where Cretan dishes and Greek words survive in their grandchildren's kitchens. On Day 8, Rhodes was untouched, because in 1923 it belonged to Italy, not Greece, and the exchange applied only to Greece and Turkey. And here in Istanbul, the Greek Orthodox community was exempted, so in 1923 it still numbered more than a hundred thousand. Most of its members left in later decades, after the riots of September 1955 and the expulsions of Greek citizens in 1964, and today a few thousand remain. Chapter 6's multi-faith city emptied in two stages: the exchange took most of the Anatolian Greeks in 1922–1923, and later pressures took most of Istanbul's.

The MicroSim below lets us apply the convention's rules to ten cases, as officials had to in 1923.

docs.title: Diagram: Who Was Exchanged in 1923?
docs.text:
Who Was Exchanged in 1923?

Type: microsim sim-id: population-exchange-1923-cases Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the rules of the 1923 population exchange convention to ten household cases, deciding whether each was sent to Greece, sent to Turkey, or not exchanged, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the Greco-Turkish War, the millet system (Chapter 6), the Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations, its exemptions for the Greek Orthodox of Istanbul, the Muslims of Western Thrace, and the Greek Orthodox of Imbros and Tenedos (all defined in the section "The Greco-Turkish War" above), and Rhodes as an Italian possession in 1923 (section "The Modern Greek State").

Evidence of Mastery: For each case, the learner chooses one of three outcomes before feedback. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct outcome column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt, including cases 3 and 4, which test the religion-not-language rule.

Misconceptions: (1) The exchange was decided by language or ethnicity (cases 3 and 4). (2) Every Greek in Turkey was exchanged, including in Istanbul (cases 1 and 2). (3) It applied to every minority, including Jews (case 7). (4) It applied to all the Greek islands, including Rhodes (case 9). (5) Refugees who had already fled in 1922 could go home once the war ended (case 10).

Instructional Rationale: Applying a written rule to concrete cases is an Apply task, and the cases are built so that the obvious guess from language or nationality is wrong. Each case's feedback quotes the rule that decides it, so the learner rebuilds the convention from its consequences.

Content:

The rules shown to the learner before case 1 (simplified from the convention):

  1. Greek Orthodox Christians living in Turkey are exchanged to Greece.
  2. Muslims living in Greece are exchanged to Turkey.
  3. People of these two groups who had already left since 1912 count as exchanged, and may not return.
  4. Exempt: the Greek Orthodox established in Istanbul before October 30, 1918; the Muslims of Western Thrace; the Greek Orthodox of Imbros and Tenedos.
  5. The exchange applies only to Greece and Turkey.

The three outcomes: Sent to Greece; Sent to Turkey; Not exchanged.

# Case (illustrative household) Correct outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 A Greek Orthodox family whose grandparents settled in Istanbul in 1890 Not exchanged Rule 4: established in Istanbul before October 30, 1918. 2 A Greek Orthodox family that moved to Istanbul from the Black Sea coast in 1920 Sent to Greece Rule 4 covers only those established in Istanbul before October 30, 1918, so rule 1 applies. 3 A Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christian family in Cappadocia Sent to Greece Rule 1: the test was religion, not language. 4 A Greek-speaking Muslim family in Rethymno, Crete Sent to Turkey Rule 2: the test was religion, not language. 5 A Muslim family in Komotini, Western Thrace Not exchanged Rule 4: the Muslims of Western Thrace were exempt. 6 A Muslim family in Thessaloniki Sent to Turkey Rule 2: Thessaloniki was in Greece, and only Western Thrace was exempt. 7 A Sephardic Jewish family in İzmir Not exchanged Rules 1 and 2 cover only Orthodox Christians and Muslims. 8 A Greek Orthodox family on Imbros Not exchanged Rule 4: the Greek Orthodox of Imbros and Tenedos were exempt. 9 A Muslim family on Rhodes Not exchanged Rule 5: Rhodes belonged to Italy in 1923, not Greece. 10 A Greek Orthodox family from Smyrna who fled to Athens in September 1922 Sent to Greece Rule 3: those who had already left counted as exchanged and could not return.

Provenance: Rules 1–4 simplified from the Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations, signed at Lausanne on January 30, 1923, Articles 1–3 (English text on Wikisource, "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations"); the Imbros and Tenedos exemption follows the Treaty of Lausanne, Article 14, as summarized in the Wikipedia article "Population exchange between Greece and Turkey". Rule 5 and case 9 from this chapter's section "The Modern Greek State". The ten households are illustrative composites, and the sim labels them "Illustrative cases."

Rules: Ten cases in the fixed order listed. Each is answered once for scoring; a first-attempt answer is correct if and only if it equals the Correct outcome. Score is 0 to 10; mastery is score >= 8 with cases 3 and 4 both correct. The five rules stay visible throughout. After each answer, the rule number that decided the case is highlighted.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the five rules.
  2. For each case, the learner chooses an outcome.
  3. Feedback names the deciding rule, and the case joins a summary grouped by outcome.
  4. After case 10, the summary shows Sent to Greece 3, Sent to Turkey 2, Not exchanged 5.
  5. The learner should notice that half the cases were not exchanged, and that language decided none of them.

Feedback: After each first attempt: correct shows "Correct:" and the Why text; incorrect shows "Not quite. [Correct outcome]:" and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 10." At the end: if mastery is met, "You applied the convention as its officials did: by religion and by the exemptions."; otherwise, "Look again at cases 3 and 4: what did the convention test, language or faith?" A Try Again option repeats all ten.

Starting State: The five rules, the three outcomes, and case 1, with the question "Under the 1923 convention, what happens to this household?"

Chapter Anchors: Convention signed January 30, 1923; about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians and about 400,000 Muslims; exemptions for Istanbul (settled before October 30, 1918), Western Thrace, and Imbros and Tenedos; Rhodes Italian in 1923; ten cases; mastery 8 of 10.

docs.title: The Turkish War of Independence
docs.text:
The Turkish War of Independence (1919–1923) was the struggle of the Turkish nationalist movement, led by Mustafa Kemal, against the occupation and partition of Anatolia after World War I. It was larger than the war with Greece. On the eastern front, the nationalists fought the new Armenian republic in 1920. On the southern front, they fought the French in Cilicia, where the cities of Antep, Maraş, and Urfa later added honorific titles to their names, becoming Gaziantep ("Antep the Veteran"), Kahramanmaraş ("Heroic Maraş"), and Şanlıurfa ("Glorious Urfa"). On the western front they fought Greece. Meanwhile the sultan's government in occupied Istanbul still claimed authority, and for three years Turkey had two governments.

The movement's aims were set out in the National Pact (Misak-ı Millî) of January 1920, which claimed for the nation the lands with an Ottoman Muslim majority that were still held by Ottoman forces when the armistice was signed in October 1918, demanded the security of Istanbul and the Sea of Marmara, and left the future of the Arab provinces, already occupied in 1918, to their inhabitants. In April 1920 a Grand National Assembly opened in Ankara. The sultan's government signed the Treaty of Sèvres on August 10, 1920, which would have left the Turks a small state in central and northern Anatolia, and the Assembly rejected it. After the victories of 1921 and 1922, the Allies negotiated again with the Ankara government, and the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on July 24, 1923, recognized an independent Turkey with roughly its present borders. Allied troops left Istanbul in October 1923.

Worked example: reading a treaty against the Pact. Let's test one of Sèvres's terms against the National Pact and predict what Lausanne did with it. Sèvres gave Eastern Thrace, the land around Edirne on the European side, to Greece. That land had a Muslim majority and was held by Ottoman forces at the armistice, so it lay inside the Pact's claim, and the nationalists had won the war. We should predict that Lausanne reversed this term, and it did: the border was drawn on the Maritsa River, where it still runs. Now try the Arab provinces: Sèvres took them away, but the Pact had already left them out of its claim, so we should predict that Lausanne kept that term, and it did. One question, "was it inside the Pact?", predicts most of the treaty. The MicroSim below gives us ten terms to test.

docs.title: Diagram: Sèvres or Lausanne?
docs.text:
Sèvres or Lausanne?

Type: diagram sim-id: sevres-versus-lausanne Library: html Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the terms of the 1920 Treaty of Sèvres that the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne reversed from those it kept, predicting at least 8 of 10 correctly and explaining the pattern by the National Pact.

Prerequisites: the Treaty of Sèvres, the Treaty of Lausanne, the National Pact, the Grand National Assembly, the Greco-Turkish War, the Dardanelles Strait, and the capitulations (all defined in Parts One to Three above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the ten treaty terms, the learner predicts "Reversed" or "Kept" before Lausanne's term is revealed. A prediction is correct when it matches the Lausanne outcome column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. After the ten, the learner chooses which of three explanations accounts for the pattern; the correct choice is part of the evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Lausanne simply cancelled Sèvres, reversing every term. (2) Turkey regained the Arab provinces. (3) Lausanne gave Turkey full control of the Straits at once, when that came only with the Montreux Convention of 1936. (4) Rhodes became Greek at Lausanne.

Instructional Rationale: Comparing two treaties term by term and then naming the rule that sorts them is an Analyze task: the learner must find the principle, the National Pact, behind ten separate outcomes. Predicting before each reveal makes the learner use the principle rather than read the answers.

Content:

The two outcomes: Reversed (Lausanne undid the Sèvres term); Kept (Lausanne left the Sèvres term in place, in substance).

# Term Treaty of Sèvres, 1920 Treaty of Lausanne, 1923 Lausanne outcome Why (shown as feedback) 1 Smyrna (İzmir) and its region Greek administration for five years, then a possible vote on joining Greece Turkish Reversed A Turkish-majority region held at the armistice, inside the Pact, and won back in 1922. 2 Eastern Thrace (Edirne) To Greece Turkish, with the border on the Maritsa River Reversed Inside the Pact's claim; the nationalists' victory made it Turkish. 3 Imbros and Tenedos To Greece Turkish, with local self-government promised to their Greek inhabitants Reversed The islands guard the mouth of the Dardanelles, and the Pact demanded the security of Istanbul and the Sea of Marmara. 4 Armenia An independent Armenian state in eastern Anatolia, with borders to be drawn by U.S. President Wilson Not mentioned; the eastern border agreed with the Soviet republics in 1921 stands Reversed The nationalists won the eastern front in 1920, and the plan was dropped. 5 Kurdistan A plan for local autonomy, with possible later independence Not mentioned Reversed Ankara claimed these lands under the Pact, and the plan was dropped. 6 Capitulations Restored, with Allied supervision of Ottoman finances Abolished Reversed Full sovereignty was the heart of the national movement. 7 The Straits Under an international commission, demilitarized Under Turkish sovereignty but still demilitarized and supervised by an international commission Kept Lausanne kept the commission and demilitarization; full Turkish control came only with the Montreux Convention of 1936. 8 The Arab provinces Given up Given up Kept The Pact had left them out of its claim. 9 Rhodes and the Dodecanese Given up in favor of Italy Given up in favor of Italy Kept Italy had held them since 1912; they were handed to Greece only in 1947, with formal union in 1948. 10 Cyprus British annexation recognized British annexation recognized Kept Cyprus had been under British rule since 1878 and lay outside the Pact.

The three explanations offered after item 10:

  • A. Lausanne reversed whatever lay inside the National Pact's claim and kept what the Pact had not claimed. (Correct.)
  • B. Lausanne reversed every term that favored Greece and kept every term that favored Britain. (Incorrect: the Straits commission and the Dodecanese terms do not fit.)
  • C. Lausanne reversed everything, and the "kept" terms only look similar. (Incorrect: four terms stand in substance.)

Provenance: Terms from this chapter's sections "The Turkish War of Independence" and "The Dardanelles Strait", checked against the Wikipedia articles "Treaty of Sèvres" and "Treaty of Lausanne" (sections on territorial and Straits provisions) and "Misak-ı Millî". Item 4's 1921 border refers to the Treaty of Kars, per the Wikipedia article "Treaty of Kars".

Rules: Ten terms in the fixed order listed. Each prediction is made once; a first-attempt prediction is correct if and only if it equals the Lausanne outcome. Score is 0 to 10; mastery is score >= 8 and explanation A chosen. Revealing a term's Lausanne column is permanent for that attempt. The explanation question allows one choice, scored correct only for A.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees a two-column comparison with all ten Sèvres terms shown and the Lausanne column hidden.
  2. For each term in order, the learner predicts Reversed or Kept.
  3. The Lausanne term is revealed with feedback, and the row is marked with its outcome.
  4. After ten, the learner sees the tally, Reversed 6 and Kept 4, and chooses an explanation.
  5. The learner should notice that every reversed term lay inside the National Pact's claim, and every kept term lay outside it.

Feedback: After each prediction: correct shows "Correct:" and the Why text; incorrect shows "Lausanne [reversed/kept] this term:" and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 10." For the explanation: A shows "Yes: the National Pact predicts the treaty."; B and C show the incorrect reason given in Content, then reveal A. A Try Again option hides the Lausanne column and resets.

Starting State: The ten Sèvres terms visible, the Lausanne column hidden, and the question "The Turkish nationalists won the war. Which of these terms survived the peace?"

Chapter Anchors: Sèvres signed August 10, 1920; Lausanne signed July 24, 1923; National Pact of January 1920; border on the Maritsa River; Montreux Convention 1936; Rhodes Italian from 1912 and Greek from 1947; ten terms, six reversed and four kept; mastery 8 of 10.

docs.title: The Republic of Turkey
docs.text:
The Republic of Turkey is the state proclaimed by the Grand National Assembly on October 29, 1923, with Mustafa Kemal as its first president and Ankara, made the capital about two weeks earlier, as its seat of government. The sultanate had already been abolished on November 1, 1922; the last sultan, Mehmed VI, left Istanbul on a British warship on November 17. In 1924 the Republic abolished the caliphate as well. The first census, in 1927, counted about 13.6 million people; today Turkey has about 85 million.

For its first two decades the Republic was a one-party state, governed by Atatürk's Republican People's Party. Multi-party politics began after 1945, and in 1950 an election brought the opposition Democrat Party to power peacefully. The decades since have seen rapid growth, membership of NATO from 1952, and military interventions in 1960, 1971, and 1980, as well as a failed coup attempt in 2016. A referendum in 2017 changed the system from a parliamentary to a presidential one. The Republic celebrated its centenary in 2023.

Worked example: the year as a history lesson. Let's read the Turkish calendar of national holidays, which tells the Republic's founding story in order.

  • April 23, National Sovereignty and Children's Day: the Grand National Assembly opened in Ankara on April 23, 1920. Atatürk dedicated the day to children, and children take over seats in parliament.
  • May 19, Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day: he landed at Samsun on May 19, 1919.
  • July 15, Democracy and National Unity Day: the failed coup attempt of 2016.
  • August 30, Victory Day: the decisive battle of 1922.
  • October 29, Republic Day: the proclamation of 1923.

Add the two great religious festivals, the Ramazan Bayramı at the end of the fast and the Kurban Bayramı at the time of the pilgrimage, and the calendar holds both halves of modern Turkey, the Republic and the faith. November 10 is not a holiday, but, as we will see, it may be the most solemn day of all.

docs.title: Atatürk's Reforms
docs.text:
Atatürk's reforms (in Turkish, Atatürk devrimleri) are the changes in law, religion, dress, language, and daily life that the Republic made between 1922 and 1938 to build a secular, Western-style nation-state. They were carried out from the top, quickly, by a government that tolerated little opposition. The main steps came in a rush.

  • 1924: the caliphate abolished on March 3; on the same day all schools, including the medreses of Chapter 5, were placed under the Ministry of Education, and the ministry of religious law and endowments was replaced by a Presidency of Religious Affairs. The religious courts were closed the next month.
  • 1925: the fez banned and the brimmed hat required for men; the dervish lodges closed.
  • 1926: the international calendar and clock adopted from January 1; a civil code based on Switzerland's ended polygamy and made civil marriage the law.
  • 1928: Islam removed as the state religion from the constitution; the new alphabet adopted.
  • 1930 and 1934: women given the vote in local and then national elections.
  • 1932: the call to prayer required in Turkish, as Chapter 5 described, until 1950.
  • 1934: surnames required by law.
  • 1935: Sunday, rather than Friday, made the weekly day of rest.

Worked example: a clerk in 1920 and in 1935. Let's follow one imaginary Istanbul office clerk through the reforms and see how much of his ordinary day changed in fifteen years. The table sets the two days side by side.

In 1920 In 1935 The reform behind it He wears a fez He wears a brimmed hat Hat Law, 1925 His watch is set to alaturka time, in which the day's hours are counted from sunset His watch shows the international 24-hour day Clock law, effective 1926 His letters are dated by the Islamic and Ottoman fiscal calendars His letters are dated 1935 Calendar law, effective 1926 He is known as Ahmed Efendi, son of Mehmed He is Ahmed Yılmaz, a surname he chose Surname Law, 1934 He writes in the Arabic script He writes in the Latin-based Turkish alphabet Alphabet law, 1928 His day off is Friday His day off is Sunday Weekend law, 1935 His wife cannot vote His wife has voted in a national election Women's suffrage, 1934

Almost nothing in the clerk's day was left untouched, from his head to his watch to his name. That is why historians call the reforms a revolution, and why they are still argued about. To supporters they made Turkey modern, open, and equal for women. To critics they were imposed on a pious people without their consent, and they cut the country off from its past. Both views are held in Turkey today, often within one family.

docs.title: Secularism in Turkey
docs.text:
Secularism in Turkey, called laiklik 🔊 Pronounce lah-eek-LEEK, from the French laïcité, is the constitutional principle, written into the constitution in 1937, that the state and its law are not based on religion. It works differently from the separation of church and state in the United States. Rather than staying out of religion, the Turkish state manages it. The Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet), created in 1924, runs the country's mosques, employs their imams, and sends out a sermon for Friday prayers each week. For decades, laiklik also meant limits on religious expression in public life, such as a ban on the headscarf in universities and government offices, lifted in stages after 2010. How much the state should promote, restrain, or stay neutral about religion is one of the central questions of Turkish politics.

A State That Runs the Mosques

Notice the paradox: the Republic that made religion a private matter also put the mosques on the state payroll. Think of laiklik as the state holding the steering wheel of religion rather than leaving the car. Once we see that, the Diyanet's prayer-time app from Chapter 5 and the 1932 Turkish call to prayer make sense as the same idea.

docs.title: Faith in Modern Turkey
docs.text: Faith in modern Turkey describes how religion is practiced in today's secular republic. Nearly all Turks are Muslim by background, most of them Sunni, but practice ranges from daily prayer to none at all, and the streets of one Istanbul neighborhood can hold both. A large Alevi minority, estimated at anywhere from about a tenth to a fifth of the population, follows a distinct tradition and worships in a cemevi, a gathering house, rather than a mosque. Christians and Jews together number well under one percent. On a Sunday morning in Istanbul, the Divine Liturgy is sung at the Patriarchal Church of St. George in Fener, Mass is said at the Catholic Church of St. Anthony of Padua on İstiklal Avenue, and the noon call to prayer sounds over both, a small reminder of the multi-faith city of Chapter 6.

docs.title: Hagia Sophia as Mosque
docs.text: Hagia Sophia as mosque refers to the two periods in which the great church has served as a mosque: from 1453, when Mehmed II made it the empire's chief mosque, to 1934, and again since 2020. Chapter 4's table lays out its four lives, and the signs of the first mosque period are the ones we saw on Day 2: the minarets added over the following century or so, the mihrab turned toward Mecca, the minbar, and the great roundels. Its conversion to a museum in 1934, by a cabinet decision signed during the busiest years of the reforms, belonged to the same program as the alphabet and the hat. Today it is again a working mosque, with prayers five times a day, while foreign visitors pay to follow the gallery route.

docs.title: The Hagia Sophia Status Debate
docs.text: The Hagia Sophia status debate is the continuing argument over whether the building should be a mosque, a museum, or something else, and who should decide. Chapter 4 worked through it as a case of contested history: the dates are agreed, and their meaning is not. Seen from Day 5, the debate is also an argument about Atatürk's legacy. For many religious Turks, the 1934 museum was a wound imposed by a secular state, and its reversal in 2020 restored the conquest's mosque. For many secular Turks, the museum was the young Republic's gesture of openness to the world, and its reversal a step away from Atatürk's Turkey. For Orthodox Christians, it remains their mother church. We do not need to choose a side to understand why each side cares so much.

docs.title: Atatürk Memorial Day
docs.text:
Atatürk Memorial Day is November 10, the anniversary of Atatürk's death in Dolmabahçe Palace at 9:05 AM in 1938, at the age of 57. At 9:05 AM every year, sirens sound across Turkey, and the country stops for a minute of silence: people stand still in the streets, drivers stop their cars on the highways and get out, and classes and offices fall silent. Crowds visit his mausoleum, Anıtkabir 🔊 Pronounce ah-nuht-kah-BEER, in Ankara, and the room where he died at Dolmabahçe. A clock in that room still shows 9:05. Because we arrived on November 11, we saw the city the day after, still hung with flags and his portrait.

Respect Is the Law Here

Atatürk's portrait hangs in shops, offices, and taxis, and Turkish law protects his memory: insulting it is a crime. A joke or a careless remark that would pass at home can give real offense here. Treat his image as we would a national flag, and if a conversation turns to him, listen and ask rather than judge.

docs.title: Part Five: Istanbul on a Sunday
The Turkish Economy Today
docs.text:
The Turkish economy today is one of the twenty largest in the world, an economy of about 85 million people that makes cars, appliances, textiles, and steel, grows much of the world's hazelnuts and dried apricots, and welcomes around 50 million foreign visitors a year. It has been in a customs union with the European Union since 1996, and much of what it makes is sold in Europe. Istanbul alone produces about 30 percent of the country's output. The weak point of recent years has been inflation: prices rose by more than 80 percent in the year to late 2022, and the lira has lost most of its value against the dollar since 2018, which, as Chapter 3 noted, is why prices on menus change so often.

Worked example: living with high inflation. Let's see what high inflation means for the people we meet, using illustrative round numbers. Suppose a lunch costs 500 lira today and prices rise 50 percent a year. Next year the same lunch costs 750 lira, and the year after, 1,125: more than double in two years. At home, at 3 percent a year, a $20 lunch becomes $20.60 and then about $21.22. A salary that is raised once a year falls further behind every month, a lease agreed in lira loses value to the landlord, and savings kept in lira melt. That is why many Turkish families save in gold or in foreign currency, why rents and wages are renegotiated often, and why the price of a glass of tea is a topic of everyday conversation. For us as visitors, the lira's fall makes Turkey inexpensive; for the waiter, it can make life hard. A tip in lira, left in cash as Chapter 3 advised, matters more than its size suggests.

docs.title: Daily Life in Istanbul
docs.text:
Daily life in Istanbul is the routine of a city of about 15.7 million people, nearly a fifth of Turkey's population, stretched along both shores of the Bosphorus. Millions of people commute every day between Europe and Asia, by ferry, by three bridges, by a road tunnel, and by the Marmaray railway tunnel under the strait, opened in 2013. Sunday is the day for a long serpme kahvaltı, a "spread" breakfast of many small dishes, for walks along the Bosphorus at Ortaköy and Bebek, and for football, where the city's three great clubs, Galatasaray, Fenerbahçe, and Beşiktaş, divide families and neighborhoods. The city's street cats are fed and sheltered by whole streets. Under the routine lies a worry everyone shares: Istanbul sits near a major fault, and since the earthquake of 1999 east of the city, the question of whether a building is earthquake-safe is part of choosing where to live.

One Card for the Whole City

Here's a shortcut for our last day: buy an İstanbulkart from a machine at any tram or ferry stop, load it with lira, and use it for trams, ferries, the metro, and the funicular. One card can pay for two people; just tap it once for each of us. A Sunday ferry to Üsküdar and back costs less than a coffee and gives the best view of the city we are leaving.

docs.title: Practical Notes for Day 5
docs.text:
• Order of the day. Walk up the shore from Galataport to Dolmabahçe Palace for its morning opening, about half an hour on foot or a short tram ride to Kabataş. Allow two to three hours for the state rooms and the harem. In the afternoon, either take a taxi to Fener to see the Patriarchate and its closed gate (the Sunday liturgy is in the morning), or stay close to the ship: the Istanbul Modern art museum stands at Galataport itself.
  • All-aboard. The ship sails at 6:00 PM. Check the all-aboard time in the daily program, usually 30 minutes to an hour before departure, and be back early; Sunday traffic along the shore can be slow.
  • Closures. The Grand Bazaar is closed on Sundays. Dolmabahçe is closed on Mondays, not Sundays, so today is fine. Photography inside the palace has long been restricted; follow the guards' instructions, and check hours and tickets on the day.
  • Weather and light. Expect an afternoon around 15–16 °C (59–61 °F) and the chance of rain. Sunset is about 5:45 PM, so sailaway comes at dusk: from the top deck, watch Topkapı, Hagia Sophia, and the Blue Mosque pass in silhouette as the ship turns into the Sea of Marmara.
  • Food. A Sunday serpme kahvaltı near the palace, or a last balık ekmek by the water at Eminönü.
  • Tomorrow. Day 6 docks at Çanakkale at 9:00 AM for Troy and Gallipoli. Read Chapter 8 tonight, and if you wake early, look out for the narrowing strait.

docs.title: Learning for All: A New Alphabet and a Nation at School
docs.text: On the evening of August 9, 1928, at a party gathering in Gülhane Park, at Sarayburnu below the walls of Topkapı, Mustafa Kemal stood up and announced that the Turkish nation would write with new letters. Within five months the new alphabet was the law, the newspapers were printed in it, and adults across the country were sitting in classrooms to learn it. Chapter 6 ended with Müteferrika's books unsold because too few people could read them, and with the promise that the circle would finally widen. This is that story, together with what it cost, and how uncertain the numbers behind it are.

docs.title: The Alphabet Reform of 1928
docs.text:
The alphabet reform of 1928 replaced the Arabic script, which had been used to write Turkish for most of a thousand years, with a Latin-based alphabet of 29 letters designed to fit Turkish sounds. A commission of scholars and writers prepared it over the summer of 1928. After the announcement in Gülhane, Mustafa Kemal toured the provinces with a portable blackboard, and photographs show him chalking letters in front of crowds. The Grand National Assembly passed the law on November 1, 1928. Newspapers switched to the new letters from December 1, government offices in the following months, and printing books in the Arabic script ended.

The new alphabet keeps the letters English readers know, drops q, w, and x, and adds six letters for Turkish sounds. It has one letter for each sound, and every letter is always pronounced the same way, which is what makes it easy to learn. The table shows the letters that differ from English.

Letter Sounds like Example Meaning c j in jam cami (jah-MEE) mosque ç ch in church çay (chai) tea ş sh in ship şehir (sheh-HEER) city ğ lengthens the vowel before it; not pronounced on its own dağ (daah) mountain ı (no dot) a short, unrounded "uh" kapı (kah-PUH) gate i, İ (dotted) ee in see İstanbul Istanbul ö like German ö, the vowel of her with rounded lips gör see! ü like German ü, ee with rounded lips gül rose

Worked example: five words, two scripts, revisited. Let's go back to Chapter 6's five words, which shared two spellings in the Ottoman script. In the new alphabet they are kol (arm), kul (servant), kör (blind), gör (see!), and gür (abundant): five different spellings for five different words. The eight vowels, a, e, ı, i, o, ö, u, ü, each have their own letter, and k and g are separate letters, so nothing is left for the reader to guess. Now try two signs we pass today: Giriş (gee-REESH) on the way into Dolmabahçe means "entrance," and Çıkış (chuh-KUHSH) on the way out means "exit." A beginner who knows the eight letters in the table can sound out any Turkish word on the first day, which no beginner in the Ottoman script could do. That is what the reformers meant to give the nation: a script whose first step takes weeks, not years.

The reform had real costs, and they were felt for generations. Within one generation, most Turks could no longer read their grandparents' letters, the inscriptions on Ottoman fountains and gravestones, or the millions of books and documents written before 1928. The poem carved on the Fountain of Ahmed III, just outside the Imperial Gate of Topkapı that we walked through on Day 3, is unreadable to most Istanbulites today. A campaign from 1932 onward to replace Arabic and Persian words with Turkish ones widened the gap, so that even an Ottoman text printed in the new letters can be hard to understand. And the reform was imposed from the top by a one-party government, without a vote of the people, and the Arabic script was banned from public use. In recent years Ottoman Turkish has returned as a school subject in some Turkish schools, and how much of it every Turk should learn is itself part of today's politics.

docs.title: The Nation's Schools
docs.text:
The Nation's Schools (Millet Mektepleri 🔊 Pronounce mil-LET mek-tep-leh-REE) were the free adult literacy classes opened across Turkey on January 1, 1929, to teach the new alphabet to the whole adult population. They met in the evenings in school buildings, coffeehouses, and village rooms, and soldiers learned in the army. Adults who could not read, roughly those between 16 and 45, were expected to attend a few months of classes, and they received a certificate when they passed. Mustafa Kemal was named the schools' Head Teacher (Başöğretmen) on November 24, 1928, the day Turkey still celebrates as Teachers' Day. By the government's own count, more than a million adults earned certificates in the schools' first years. In the 1930s their work passed to the People's Houses, community centers opened in 1932, and from 1940 the Village Institutes trained teachers from village families to go home and teach.

Run Chapter 2's four-step pattern on the reform, and it fits closely.

  1. Locked up: reading Turkish in the Arabic script took years of schooling, and most people never had them.
  2. Opened: a script that could be learned in weeks, with free classes for every adult.
  3. Resisted: the scholars, calligraphers, and religious teachers whose learning lived in the old script, and many ordinary pious people who saw the Arabic letters as the letters of the Quran, though under a one-party government resistance had little room.
  4. Never all the way: the classes reached towns faster than villages and men faster than women, many adults who passed lost the skill without books to practice on, and the generation that learned the new letters lost the old ones.

docs.title: Literacy Rate Uncertainty
docs.text:
Literacy rate uncertainty is the margin of doubt in any count of how many people could read, which comes from how literacy was defined, who was counted, and who did the counting. Chapter 2 gave Turkey's literacy before the reform as roughly one person in ten. That figure comes from the census of 1927, the year before the reform, which is usually quoted as about 10.6 percent, far lower among women and in villages. The census of 1935 found about one person in five, and today well over 95 percent of Turkish adults can read. The direction of the change is not in doubt. The exact starting point is less certain than the neat number suggests.

Worked example: one village, three literacy rates. Let's take an illustrative village of 1,000 people in 1927 and count its readers three ways. Of the 1,000, 300 are children under seven. Of the 700 others, 90 can read and write Ottoman Turkish, 40 more learned to recite the Quran from its Arabic letters but cannot read a letter in Turkish, and 10 read only Greek. Counted over the whole population, with only the first group as literate, the rate is 90 ÷ 1,000 = 9.0 percent. Counted over people aged seven and over, it is 90 ÷ 700 ≈ 12.9 percent. Counting everyone aged seven and over who could read any script, it is 140 ÷ 700 = 20.0 percent. The same village gives 9, 13, or 20 percent depending on three choices that a census report rarely explains. The real census asked people to report their own ability, with no test, which adds a fourth uncertainty.

The table lists the questions to ask of any historical literacy figure, with the answers for Turkey's 1927 count.

Question Why it matters Turkey, 1927 What counted as literate? Reading only, or reading and writing; reciting or understanding Self-reported reading and writing, with no test Which script or language? Readers of other scripts may be left out Mostly the Arabic script; most Greek and Armenian readers were already gone Out of whom? All ages, or adults only, changes the rate a great deal Quoted figures do not always say whether young children are included Who counted, and why? A new government has reasons to stress how much it improved The Republic's new statistics office, a year before the reform What is it compared with? Earlier estimates may rest on weaker evidence still Ottoman-era estimates rest largely on school records and travelers' impressions

None of this means the reform did not work. It means that "one in ten" is a census answer to a particular question, asked by a government with a stake in the result, and that historians who argue Ottoman reading was somewhat more common in the cities are not being contrary. Chapter 4's primary-source test applies to numbers as much as to stories.

The alphabet reform holds three lessons for AI in education. The first is the lesson of Chapter 2: lowering the cost of the first step widens the circle. A script that could be learned in weeks did more for Turkish literacy than three centuries of presses, and an AI tutor that speaks to each learner in plain language and at their own pace could be that kind of simpler interface to knowledge. The second is a warning about how change is made. The reform moved a whole nation in a few years because a one-party state commanded it, and it left a generation cut off from its own written past. Every large change carries losses as well as gains, which AI-Native Schools discusses through William Bridges' idea of endings in Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns, and national mandates, as its chapter Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption shows with a recent AI textbook rollout, can provoke the resistance they try to skip.

The third lesson is about measurement: a claim that a new tool raised learning deserves the same questions as the 1927 census, from what was counted to who did the counting. There is also a hopeful twist. Researchers are now training text-recognition systems on Ottoman script, so the technology of our own time may reopen the archives that the reform of 1928 closed.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Ottoman decline was a two-century retreat from Vienna (1683) to 1922, driven by military defeat, debt, and nationalism, and met by real reform; Dolmabahçe Palace (1843–1856) and the debt default of 1875 tell the story together.
  • Ottoman rule in Greece lasted from the late 14th century to 1912, organized through the Orthodox millet; the "secret school" is probably a legend.
  • The Greek War of Independence (1821–1830) began in the Peloponnese, cost the Patriarch Gregory V his life at the gate in Fener that is still closed, and was won at Navarino in 1827.
  • The modern Greek state began as a small kingdom in 1832 and grew for 115 years: Athens and Delphi in 1832, Heraklion in 1913, Rhodes in 1947.
  • The Dardanelles Strait, about 61 km long and narrowest at Çanakkale, is crossed tonight on our way to Day 6.
  • World War I drew the empire in through the Dardanelles in 1914 and ended it; the Armenians suffered deportation and mass death in 1915.
  • The Gallipoli Campaign of 1915 made the name of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (1881–1938), born in Salonica, who led the national movement from 1919.
  • The Greco-Turkish War (1919–1922) ended with the burning of Smyrna and the population exchange of 1923, decided by religion, not language.
  • The Turkish War of Independence (1919–1923) reversed the Treaty of Sèvres wherever the National Pact made a claim, and the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) recognized modern Turkey.
  • The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on October 29, 1923. Atatürk's reforms changed law, dress, the calendar, names, and the alphabet in fifteen years.
  • Secularism in Turkey (laiklik) means the state manages religion through the Diyanet; faith in modern Turkey ranges from devout Sunni and Alevi practice to none.
  • Hagia Sophia as a mosque (1453–1934 and since 2020) and the Hagia Sophia status debate are also an argument about Atatürk's legacy.
  • Atatürk Memorial Day, November 10, stops the country at 9:05 AM.
  • The Turkish economy today is large and industrial but has lived with high inflation; daily life in Istanbul runs on ferries, breakfasts, and football for 15.7 million people.
  • The alphabet reform of 1928 gave Turkish 29 letters, one per sound, and the Nation's Schools taught adults to read them, at the cost of cutting a generation off from the old script.
  • Literacy rate uncertainty reminds us that "one in ten" depends on what was counted, out of whom, and by whom.

From Sick Man to Republic

You can now trace the empire's retreat from Vienna to Lausanne, explain why Rhodes, Crete, and Athens became Greek in different generations, and apply the 1923 exchange rule that sorted people by faith. You can also sound out a Turkish sign and ask the right questions of a literacy statistic. Next stop: Troy and Gallipoli, where we stand on the ridges where Mustafa Kemal made his name and the mound where Homer's war was fought.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Day 6 (Monday, November 16) docks at Çanakkale. The morning at Troy covers the Bronze Age collapse, the Hittites and Wilusa, the nine cities of the Hisarlik mound, Calvert and Schliemann, and how Homer's oral epics blend myth and history. Its Learning for All note follows the Greek alphabet, which added vowels and made reading easier to learn, so that Homer could finally be written down. The afternoon turns to Gallipoli, the Anzac forces, the Çanakkale Martyrs' Memorial, Atatürk's 'Johnnies and Mehmets' words, and how cultural memory shapes a battlefield today.

docs.title: A Day on Both Shores of the Hellespont
docs.text:
Day 6, Monday, November 16, begins in the narrows of the Dardanelles. The Viking Star docks at Çanakkale at 9:00 AM and sails again at 4:00 PM, which gives us seven hours on the strait that Chapter 7 crossed in the dark. From the ship we can see both continents at once: Çanakkale and the Asian shore on one side, and across water little more than a kilometer and a half wide, the hills of the Gallipoli Peninsula in Europe. About 30 km south of the town, on a low ridge above a farming plain, lies Troy.

Early morning on the Dardanelles, just after sunrise. Photo by Dan McCreary

The two halves of the day sit more than three thousand years apart, but they ask the same question. At Troy, which we visit in the morning, a city burned around 1180 BCE, and Greek singers carried the memory of a war there for five centuries before anyone wrote it down. At Gallipoli, in the afternoon, two empires and two young nations fought in 1915, and the memory of that fight is still being shaped, carved into stone, and argued over. In both places we will be asking how a war becomes a story, and what happens to the truth on the way.

Windy Ilios and the Cove of the Anzacs

Today we climb a mound with nine cities inside it, meet the gods who took sides in the most famous war ever sung, and stand on a beach where former enemies now share the same graves. By sailaway, we will know why Homer called Troy windy, and why an inscription on that beach is both treasured and doubted. Look closer.

The chapter has five parts. Part One climbs the mound at Hisarlık 🔊 Pronounce hih-sar-LUHK and meets the people who dug it. Part Two places Troy in the Bronze Age world of the Hittites and follows that world through its collapse into the Greek Dark Age. Part Three turns to the gods, the war of legend, and Homer, and asks how much of the story is history. Part Four crosses the strait to Gallipoli, the Anzacs, and the memorials. Part Five looks at how Çanakkale lives today from all this memory. The Learning for All note then follows Homer from the singer's memory to the written page.

docs.title: Part One: The Mound at Hisarlık
Shore Excursion
docs.text: A shore excursion is an organized trip ashore sold or included by a cruise line during a port call, usually by coach with a licensed local guide, timed to bring passengers back before the ship sails. Chapter 6 showed how port times frame a cruise day; the excursion is how most passengers fill them. Its strengths are real on a day like this one: Troy and Gallipoli are on opposite shores of a strait, neither is in walking distance of the pier, and a guide who knows the sites turns rubble into a story. Its weakness is the one Chapter 2 named. Everyone arrives at the same gate at the same hour, and the day runs to the coach's clock, not to our curiosity. Seven hours is not enough to see Troy, cross to Gallipoli, and come back without hurrying, so whatever we choose, today rewards reading ahead. Check the ship's daily program for which sites each excursion visits and when its coaches return.

docs.title: Troy
docs.text:
Troy is the Bronze Age city in northwest Anatolia, near the mouth of the Dardanelles, that Greek legend remembers as the city besieged by the Greeks in the Trojan War. The ancient Greeks called it both Ilios (or Ilion) and Troia; the Romans called it Ilium. It sat on the last ridge before the sea, overlooking a plain crossed by the river Scamander (today the Karamenderes) and, in the Bronze Age, a bay that reached much closer to the city than the coast does now. Over the centuries the river filled that bay with silt, and the shoreline moved several kilometers away.

The Trojan plain seen from the citadel. Photo by Dan McCreary

Worked example: why a city here? Let's read the map the way Chapter 1 taught us. Troy stands a few kilometers from the entrance to the Dardanelles, a chokepoint between the Aegean and the Black Sea. A strong current flows out of the strait, and for much of the sailing season the wind blows from the north-northeast, straight down it. A Bronze Age ship, with a square sail and oars, could not easily beat upstream against both. So ships waiting to enter had good reason to shelter in the bay below Troy, sometimes for weeks, until the wind turned. The excavator Manfred Korfmann argued that Troy grew rich from those waiting ships: water, food, repairs, and perhaps tolls. That is a theory, not a recorded fact, but the wind is real. Homer gave Troy a fixed epithet, ēnemoessa, "windy," and on a November afternoon on the citadel, we will probably understand why.

docs.title: Stratigraphy
docs.text:
Chapter 1 introduced stratigraphy, the study of the layers that build up where people live in one place for a long time, and Chapter 4 taught us to read a city's layers and a ruin's history. At Troy we get to apply both on the most famous stratified site in the world. Two rules do most of the work. The first, the law of superposition, says that in undisturbed ground a layer lies above anything older and below anything younger. The second is that people dig: a later foundation, pit, or trench can cut down through earlier layers, so a cut must be dated by the youngest layer it cuts through, not by the oldest material it exposes.

Worked example: reading a trench wall. Let's stand at the great north-south trench through the middle of the mound and read the earth wall in front of us from the top down. At the top lie loose soil and the marble fragments of Roman Ilium. Below them, stone house walls run in and out of the cut, each set resting on the rubble of the one before. Here and there a band of dark ash or burned mud brick runs across the section: a fire, the end of one settlement. Near the bottom, the walls are smaller and made of rough stone and mud brick, the houses of the first Troy, around 3000 BCE. Now the second rule: the trench itself is a layer. It cuts through all the others, so it is younger than all of them, and we know its date exactly, because Heinrich Schliemann dug it in the early 1870s. Seen this way, even the damage at Troy is evidence.

Find the Trench First

Here's a shortcut for the whole site: find Schliemann's great trench early on the walking route and spend two minutes reading its walls from the top down. It is the one place where all the cities appear in a single cross-section, and every stop after it will make more sense.

docs.title: The Hisarlık Mound
docs.text:
The Hisarlık Mound is the artificial hill near the village of Tevfikiye that holds the ruins of Troy. Its Turkish name means "place of the fortress." A mound like this is what archaeologists call a tell, from an Arabic word for hill: a hill made by people, built up over thousands of years of houses, walls, and rubbish, each generation leveling the ruins of the last and building on top. At Hisarlık the layers of human life inside the mound span roughly 3,500 years, from about 3000 BCE to about 500 CE.

For most of its history, nobody doubted that this hill was Ilion. Greek settlers lived on it from about 700 BCE; Alexander the Great sacrificed here in 334 BCE at what he was shown as the tomb of Achilles; and Roman emperors, who claimed descent from the Trojan prince Aeneas, rebuilt it as Ilium. Only in the 18th and 19th centuries, when the site had long been abandoned, did scholars begin to argue over where Troy had been, and several other hills were proposed. The case for Hisarlık was made with a spade.

Excavated walls of Troy. Photo by Dan McCreary

docs.title: The Nine Cities of Troy
docs.text:
The Nine Cities of Troy are the nine main settlement layers that archaeologists number from the bottom up, Troy I through Troy IX, each with sub-phases marked by letters (Troy VIIa, VIIb, and so on). Chapter 1's table gave their dates, from about 3000 BCE for Troy I to about 500 CE for the last of Roman Ilium. Today we see them not in order but as a walk, because the site's path loops through the citadel and passes the layers wherever they happen to be exposed. The table below reorganizes them as the route meets them.

What we see on the route Layer Approximate date The sloping, finely fitted stone wall and the East Gate Troy VI c. 1750–1300 BCE The great stone tower on the northeast corner Troy VI c. 1750–1300 BCE Small, crowded houses built against the inside of the Troy VI walls Troy VIIa c. 1300–1180 BCE The stone ramp Schliemann took for Homer's Scaean Gate Troy II c. 2550–2300 BCE The deep trench through the middle of the mound Cut in the 1870s Exposes Troy I to IX Marble pieces of the Temple of Athena Troy VIII–IX Hellenistic and Roman The sanctuary below the southwest wall Troy VIII–IX, with older roots c. 700 BCE onward The odeon (small theater) and the council house Troy IX Roman, 1st–2nd century CE

The same walk is a lesson from Chapter 4: an old object is not an old layer. The odeon is the newest thing in the citadel, though it is the most complete, and the oldest walls, at the bottom of the trench, are the hardest to see.

The odeon (small theater) at Troy. Photo by Dan McCreary

docs.title: Troy VI and VIIa
docs.text: Troy VI and VIIa are the two layers of Late Bronze Age Troy that are the leading candidates for Homer's city. Troy VI, from about 1750 to 1300 BCE, was the grandest Troy: a citadel ringed by a sloping limestone wall about 5 m thick, built in neat sections with shallow offsets, and large houses on terraces inside. Excavations from 1988 onward, led by Manfred Korfmann, found a lower town below the citadel, protected by a defensive ditch cut into the rock, which suggests a city of several thousand people. Not every scholar accepts that the lower town was so large; the historian Frank Kolb argued in 2001 and 2002 that Korfmann had made Troy sound grander than the evidence allowed. Troy VI ended around 1300 BCE in damage that looks like an earthquake: collapsed walls, but no great fire. The survivors rebuilt, cramming small houses against the walls and burying storage jars in the floors, the look of a city expecting a siege. That city, Troy VIIa, was destroyed around 1180 BCE by fire, and in its ruins excavators found arrowheads and human remains. Whether that destruction was the work of Greeks, or of raiders, or of a war we cannot name, the stones do not say.

docs.title: Frank Calvert
docs.text: Frank Calvert (1828–1908) was a member of an English family living at the Dardanelles, where he served as a consular agent, and the first person to dig at Hisarlık in search of Homer's Troy. The Calverts owned a farm near the site and part of the mound itself. From the 1850s, Frank studied the Trojan plain, and in the early 1860s he dug trial trenches on his part of Hisarlık and found ancient walls. He became convinced that Troy lay inside, but he lacked the money for a full excavation. In 1868 a wealthy visitor came to see him, listened, and took up the idea. That visitor wrote Calvert almost out of the story for a century, until historians, using the two men's letters, gave him back his share of the credit.

docs.title: Heinrich Schliemann
docs.text:
Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890) was the German businessman who excavated Troy from 1871 to 1890 and made it world famous. He had grown rich in trade, in Russia and, briefly, in gold-rush California, and spent his fortune proving that Homer's world was real. He dug in big seasons with large crews, and his huge trench through the mound, as Chapter 1 explained, destroyed parts of the layers closest to Homer's age. He also learned: from 1882 the architect Wilhelm Dörpfeld worked beside him and brought careful recording, and before Schliemann died he had begun to suspect that the Troy of the legend lay higher up the mound than he first thought.

Schliemann's own life story deserves the myth-versus-history test of Chapter 4. In his later books he wrote that, as a boy of eight, he saw a picture of Troy burning and promised his father he would find it. His letters and diaries from his early life, which historians have studied closely, say nothing of the kind; the story appears only after he was famous. Like the line about Solomon at Hagia Sophia, it tells us what Schliemann wanted his life to mean.

docs.title: Priam's Treasure
docs.text:
Priam's Treasure is the hoard of gold, silver, and bronze objects, including two gold diadems made of thousands of small gold pieces, that Schliemann found at Troy in 1873 and named after Homer's king of Troy. It came from Troy II, about a thousand years too early for Priam. Schliemann smuggled it out of the Ottoman Empire, breaking his agreement to share finds, and the Ottoman government sued him; he paid a settlement. He gave most of it to Berlin in 1881. At the end of the Second World War, Soviet troops took it from Berlin to Moscow, and it vanished until 1993, when Russia confirmed that it was in the Pushkin Museum, where it remains. Some pieces are in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. Schliemann published a famous photograph of his wife, Sophia, wearing the diadems, and wrote that she had carried the treasure away in her shawl; he later admitted she had been in Athens at the time.

The Name on the Label Is Not a Date

A common trap at Troy is to trust a name: "Priam's Treasure," "the Scaean Gate," "the tomb of Achilles." Each was named by someone who hoped to find Homer, before the layers were dated. When you meet a Homeric name on a label, look for the layer number beside it, and believe the number.

docs.title: Site Museum
docs.text:
A site museum is a museum built at or beside an archaeological site to display the objects found there, so that visitors can see the finds and the place together. Its great advantage is context. A pot in a national museum is one pot among thousands; the same pot a few hundred meters from the house where it was buried tells the story of that house. A site museum also keeps some of the benefit of a site's fame in its own region, in jobs and visitors. Its limits are practical: it holds only what has stayed nearby, and the most famous finds from the oldest excavations are often far away, in national capitals or foreign museums.

Worked example: where are Troy's finds? Let's follow the objects from the mound and count the countries.

  • Russia: Schliemann's gold, taken from Berlin to Moscow in 1945.
  • Germany: other finds from Schliemann's digs that stayed in Berlin.
  • Turkey: the Ottoman government's share of Schliemann's finds, in Istanbul, and everything excavated since.
  • United States: some finds from Carl Blegen's American excavations of 1932 to 1938, divided under the rules of the time; and, until 2012, a group of gold jewelry said to come from the Troy region, bought by the University of Pennsylvania Museum in 1966 and sent back to Turkey in 2012.

So a visitor who wanted to see "Troy" in one room would need tickets in four countries. A site museum cannot reunite all of that, but it can show what the region still holds, and that is what Troy finally built.

docs.title: The Troy Museum
docs.text: The Troy Museum (Troya Müzesi) opened in 2018 just outside the archaeological site, after decades in which Troy's finds were scattered among other museums. Its building is a large square block clad in rust-colored steel, a color chosen to echo the earth of the excavations. Its collections come from Troy and the surrounding region, the Troad, and its most striking piece is the Polyxena Sarcophagus, a marble coffin of about 520–500 BCE found in the region in 1994, carved with the sacrifice of the Trojan princess Polyxena at the end of the war. The jewelry returned from Philadelphia is here too. Allow an hour, and if time is short, go after the site, so that the objects land on places you have just walked.

docs.title: Part Two: Troy in a Bronze Age World
The Hittite Empire
docs.text: The Hittite Empire was the great Bronze Age state of central Anatolia, which ruled from its capital, Hattusa, near today's village of Boğazkale, about 150 km east of Ankara, from about 1650 to about 1180 BCE. At its height it reached from the Aegean coast to northern Syria. The Hittites spoke an Indo-European language, the oldest one we can read, and wrote it in cuneiform, wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets. Their palace archives, found from 1906 onward, hold tens of thousands of tablets: laws, prayers, letters to other kings, and treaties. The most famous is the peace treaty made in 1259 BCE with the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II after the battle of Kadesh, one of the oldest peace treaties known; a copy hangs at the United Nations headquarters in New York. To the Hittites, western Anatolia was a frontier of small kingdoms to be bound by treaty, and that is where Troy comes in.

docs.title: Wilusa
docs.text:
Wilusa 🔊 Pronounce wih-LOO-sah is a kingdom in northwest Anatolia named in Hittite texts, which most scholars now identify with Troy. The link starts with a sound. Homer's Ilios was once Wilios: early Greek had a w sound, written with a letter called digamma, that later dropped out. Wilusa fits Wilios closely, and a place called Taruisa, named once in a Hittite list, may be Troia. The texts add more. Around 1280 BCE the Hittite king Muwatalli II made a treaty with Alaksandu, king of Wilusa, a name strikingly like Alexandros, the other name of Homer's Paris. Another letter, from a Hittite king to the king of a land called Ahhiyawa 🔊 Pronounce ah-khee-YAH-wah (most likely the Mycenaean Greeks, Homer's Achaioi), mentions an earlier quarrel between the two of them over Wilusa. And a later letter speaks of a king of Wilusa named Walmu who had been driven out and whom the Hittite king meant to restore.

None of this proves a Trojan War. It does show that in the 13th century BCE a kingdom at Troy's location was a Hittite ally, that Greeks from Ahhiyawa were active on that coast, and that Wilusa was a place where great powers quarreled. The table lists the main texts.

Hittite text Approximate date What it says about Wilusa A list of western lands under Tudhaliya I c. 1400 BCE Names Wilusiya and Taruisa among a coalition of western lands the Hittite king defeated Treaty with Alaksandu c. 1280 BCE Wilusa is a Hittite vassal; Alaksandu is its king Letter to the king of Ahhiyawa c. 1250 BCE The Hittite and Ahhiyawan kings had quarreled over Wilusa Letter about Walmu Late 13th century BCE Walmu, king of Wilusa, was driven out; the Hittite king plans to restore him

Three Names, Three Matches

If Wilusa, Ahhiyawa, and Alaksandu feel like a tongue-twister, that is normal; even specialists keep a cheat sheet. Hold on to just three matches: Wilusa for Ilios, Ahhiyawa for the Achaeans, Alaksandu for Alexandros. With those three, the table above reads like a news report from Homer's world.

docs.title: The Bronze Age Collapse
docs.text:
Chapter 1 described the Bronze Age collapse, also called the Late Bronze Age collapse: the breakdown of the connected palace world of the Eastern Mediterranean between about 1200 and 1150 BCE. Troy lets us see it from one city and then look outward. Troy VIIa burned around 1180 BCE. At about the same time, Hattusa was abandoned and the Hittite Empire disappeared from history. The great trading city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast was destroyed; its last letters speak of enemy ships. On the Greek mainland the Mycenaean palaces at Pylos and elsewhere burned, and their scribes' records stop. Egypt survived, barely: around 1177 BCE Pharaoh Ramesses III recorded on the walls of his temple at Medinet Habu a battle against invaders from the sea, the people modern historians call the Sea Peoples.

Worked example: one link breaks, then the next. Let's trace how a failure could spread, using causes historians have proposed. Suppose several years of drought, which tree rings and lake sediments suggest for parts of the region, cut harvests in Anatolia. The Hittite king, short of grain, depends on shipments from Egypt and Ugarit. Ugarit, meanwhile, is sending its ships and soldiers to help its Hittite overlord, so its own coast is undefended when raiders arrive. Palaces that ran on stored grain and bronze cannot pay their soldiers and craftsmen; the tin trade that Chapter 1's Uluburun ship carried stops; earthquakes strike cities already short of labor to rebuild. No single cause explains it, and historians still argue over which mattered most. What the dates show is that the systems were tied together, so a shock in one place became a crisis everywhere. Troy did not fall alone.

A Network Fails as a Network

Notice that the Bronze Age palaces were strong precisely because they were connected, and fragile for the same reason. Think of it like a row of ships tied together in a storm: the ropes that steady them in calm weather drag them down together when one ship goes under. That idea comes back on Crete, where a whole script died with the palaces that used it.

On Day 9, Chapter 13 tells that story at Knossos, where the Linear B tablets were baked hard by the fires that ended the palace world, and explains how they were finally read.

docs.title: The Greek Dark Age
docs.text:
The Greek Dark Age is the period from about 1100 to about 800 BCE, after the collapse of the Mycenaean palaces, when Greece had fewer people, poorer settlements, little long-distance trade, and no writing at all. Chapter 1 introduced it and warned that "dark" describes our lack of written sources more than the lives of the people. At Troy the period shows as Troy VIIb: poorer settlements on the old citadel after 1180 BCE, then, by about 950 BCE, a site nearly empty. Around 700 BCE Greek-speaking settlers from across the Aegean moved onto the hill and founded Ilion, Troy VIII, a Greek town living on top of a legend.

Worked example: what crossed the dark? Let's ask what survived three centuries without writing. Archaeology answers part of it. At Lefkandi on the island of Euboea, excavators found a building about 45 m long, from about 950 BCE, with the burials of a warrior and a richly dressed woman and four horses: a community wealthy and organized enough to honor its leaders lavishly, in the depth of the "dark." The gods crossed too: Zeus, Hera, and Poseidon are named on Mycenaean tablets before the collapse and worshipped by Greeks after it. And the epics themselves carry objects from before the dark. In the Iliad, Odysseus is given a helmet covered with rows of boars' tusks. No Greek of Homer's own day wore such a helmet, but archaeologists have found boars'-tusk helmets in Mycenaean graves of the Bronze Age. The description could only have reached Homer through song, passed from singer to singer for about five hundred years. That is our first evidence of how much an oral tradition could carry.

The end of the Dark Age also brought new places where Greeks from many communities met: Olympia, where the Games were traditionally founded in 776 BCE, and Delphi, whose sanctuary began to grow in the 8th century BCE. Chapter 18 walks through Delphi on Day 12.

docs.title: Part Three: Gods, Heroes, and the Song of Troy
The Olympian Gods
docs.text:
The Olympian gods are the twelve principal gods of the ancient Greeks, imagined as a single family living on Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece, under the rule of Zeus. They were not distant abstractions. Greeks pictured them in human form, with human passions, quarrels, favorites, and grudges, but immortal and far more powerful. Each had particular domains (the sea, the harvest, war, love, crafts), favorite places and animals, and a symbol by which an artist could show them. Each city had its own special patron, which is why Athens is named for Athena, and each god had many local festivals and sanctuaries. Chapter 1 described the Greeks as a people who "worshipped the same family of gods," and that family is one of the things that made scattered city-states feel like one civilization.

The list of twelve varied a little between places and periods, but the usual one is below. The table also shows where we meet each god on our own route.

God Domains Symbol to look for Where we meet them Zeus King of the gods; sky, weather, justice Thunderbolt, eagle Temple of Olympian Zeus, Athens (Day 13) Hera Queen of the gods; marriage, women Crown, peacock Many sanctuaries; at Troy in the Iliad Poseidon Sea, earthquakes, horses Trident Temple at Cape Sounion Demeter Grain, harvest Sheaf of wheat, torch Eleusis, near Athens Athena Wisdom, strategy in war, crafts Owl, helmet, shield (aegis) Temple of Athena at Troy; the Parthenon (Day 10) Apollo Light, music, prophecy, healing, archery Lyre, bow, laurel Delphi (Days 11–12) Artemis Hunting, wild animals, childbirth Bow, deer Ephesus (Day 7) Ares War and violence Spear, helmet Few temples of his own Aphrodite Love and beauty Dove, mirror Statues in the Athens museums Hephaestus Fire, metalwork, smiths Hammer, tongs Temple of Hephaestus, Athens Agora (Day 11) Hermes Messenger; travelers, trade, thieves Winged sandals, herald's staff Boundary markers called herms Dionysus Wine, theater, ecstasy Vine, ivy, wine cup Theater of Dionysus, Athens (Day 10)

Some lists put Hestia, goddess of the hearth, in place of Dionysus.

Worked example: the gods go to war at Troy. Let's see the Olympians in action, because the Iliad is the oldest place we can watch them. In Book 20, as the fighting reaches its peak, Zeus lifts his ban on the gods joining the battle and stays on Olympus to watch. The others go down to the plain we can see from the citadel. Hera, Athena, Poseidon, Hermes, and Hephaestus 🔊 Pronounce heh-FESS-tus go to the Greek ships. Ares, Apollo, Artemis, and Aphrodite go to the Trojans, along with Leto, the mother of Apollo and Artemis, and Xanthos, the god of the river. Now look for reasons. Three of the choices follow from a single story, the Judgment of Paris, told in the next section: Hera and Athena lost a beauty contest that Aphrodite won by promising Paris the most beautiful woman in the world. Poseidon has an old grievance: in the Iliad he recalls that an earlier Trojan king cheated him of his wages for building the city's walls. Apollo has his own: in Book 1 the Greek commander Agamemnon insults Apollo's priest, and Apollo answers with a plague on the Greek camp. So the gods take sides for the most human reasons there are: wounded pride, old debts, and favorites. Of the twelve Olympians, that makes five for the Greeks, four for the Trojans, and three outside the fight: Zeus above it, and Demeter and Dionysus, who play no part in the Iliad.

Read the Hands, Not the Faces

Want to name a god on a vase or a relief in seconds? Ignore the face, which artists made almost alike, and look at what the figure holds or wears: a trident is Poseidon, a helmet with a spear on a woman is Athena, a bow on a woman is Artemis, winged sandals are Hermes. Ancient viewers read the same symbols.

The MicroSim below asks us to sort all twelve by the side they took, using each god's domain and story.

docs.title: Diagram: The Olympian Gods at Troy
docs.text:
The Olympian Gods at Troy

Type: microsim sim-id: olympian-gods-at-troy Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of the twelve Olympian gods by the side they take in Homer's Iliad (helped the Greeks, helped the Trojans, or stayed above or outside the fight), using each god's domain and story, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first check.

Prerequisites: Olympian gods, Mount Olympus, the Iliad, the Judgment of Paris, and the Trojan War, all defined in Part Three of this chapter.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places all 12 god cards into the three bins and presses Check. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 10 of 12 correct on the first Check. Flipping a card to read its domain and symbol is exploration, not evidence. The prediction in Learner Activity step 2 is recorded but not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) The gods acted as impartial judges of right and wrong. (2) The god of war must have been on the winning side. (3) Every Olympian fought at Troy. (4) Zeus was simply a Trojan partisan.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying the gods by side forces the learner to connect each god's story (the Judgment of Paris, Poseidon's unpaid wages, Apollo's insulted priest) to a choice, which is an Understand task rather than recall of a list. A committed prediction of the totals before sorting exposes misconception 3.

Content:

Three bins, labeled exactly: "Helped the Greeks", "Helped the Trojans", "Above or outside the fight".

Twelve cards. Each card's front shows the god's name, domains, and symbol, as in the chapter's table.
